extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and policymakers interested in disinformation research
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the academic field of disinformation research: its definitions, aims, major research streams, methods, institutions, publication venues, and countermeasure approaches. Provides descriptive criteria for what the field studies and how it is organized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims of disinformation research
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinformation research is a joint project by academics and policymakers aiming 'to examine the causes and effects of various deceptions, from fake news to conspiracy theories... It also aims to develop countermeasures and policies that mitigate the spread of disinformation while protecting democratic freedoms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses both on manifestations of deception and on designing counterstrategies; explicitly includes policy-oriented goals and the protection of democratic freedoms. Research should consider both supply (how false content is produced/spread) and demand (why people consume and believe it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorenstein Center definition: study spread, impacts, and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Shorenstein Center defines disinformation research as studying 'the spread, impacts, and potential solutions to bad and misleading information in society,' including 'the causes of misinformation, how it spreads through online and offline channels, why people are susceptible..., and successful strategies for mitigating its impact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes empirical study of transmission pathways and interventions; research should link causal mechanisms (why and how) to practical mitigation strategies and policy recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic framework and research methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The field provides a systemic framework and research methods for studying multiple interrelated phenomena of deceptive practices, with particular attention to the online manipulation tools and tactics used to distort public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should adopt systematic, often interdisciplinary methods (qualitative and quantitative) to connect phenomena such as fake news and conspiracy theories to platform affordances, actors, and tactics. Methods may include bibliographic analyses, computational detection, case studies, and experimental psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation and health research (research cluster)
rubrics_metrics.description: A research cluster that examines disinformation related to health topics (e.g., COVID-19 misinformation), focusing on how false health narratives spread and how to fight them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common focal points include public health impacts, vaccine misinformation, health literacy interventions, and the role of platforms and actors in amplifying health-related falsehoods. Works often connect to health communication and medical internet research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation research in digital technologies and cybersecurity (research cluster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies the use of advanced digital technologies for internet manipulation, including bots and coordinated inauthentic behavior; aims include detection of disinformation at scale, impact measurement, and data infrastructures for studying online phenomena without compromising user privacy or data integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological priorities: scalable detection algorithms, measurement frameworks, privacy-preserving data collection, and ethical protocols. Also examines platform-level interventions and cybersecurity aspects (e.g., coordinated campaigns, botnets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation in journalism and media research (research cluster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examines strategies used for media manipulation and, in journalism, focuses on fake news and its correction via fact‑checking and media literacy; also studies how social media amplifies polarization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research evaluates journalistic corrections, fact-checker efficacy, media literacy programs, and the structural dynamics (echo chambers, algorithmic amplification) that influence news consumption and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation research in political communication and democratic governance (research cluster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the deliberate use of deception to influence political outcomes; studies consequences of disinformation on society and trust in democratic institutions and includes research into state responses to hybrid security threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes analysis of political campaigns, information warfare, policy responses (e.g., hybrid threats frameworks), and implications for democratic legitimacy. Often intersects with studies of state actors and institutional resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation in psychology and behavioral research (research cluster)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subfield that examines the cognitive processes that influence why people believe and share misinformation; key factors include cognitive biases that favor information fitting pre-existing beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical approaches use experimental psychology to study susceptibility, belief updating, persuasion, and interventions (e.g., prebunking, inoculation). Research should identify cognitive mechanisms and behavioral levers for mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinformation in business and advertising research (research cluster)
rubrics_metrics.description: Market-oriented research investigating the circulation of disinformation from a business perspective, addressing market practices that render it profitable, including overlaps between ad fraud mechanisms and revenue that funds fake news websites; includes influencer-driven misinformation for profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes economic incentives, programmatic advertising, revenue flows, ad-tech ecosystems, influencer monetization, and policy/regulatory implications for market-based countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical guidelines for conducting disinformation research
rubrics_metrics.description: The field addresses ethical guidelines for conducting disinformation research without harm, particularly when studying user data, platform content, or interventions that could affect individuals or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should prioritize privacy-preserving methods, informed consent where appropriate, minimization of harms from interventions or data releases, and transparency about limitations. Ethical considerations are especially salient for large-scale data collection and experimental interventions on platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection, measurement, and data infrastructure priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: A stated purpose in the digital-technology stream: detection of disinformation at scale, measurement of impact, and the data infrastructures required to study online disinformation while protecting privacy and data integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should balance methodological rigor with privacy and reproducibility: develop robust detection models, standardized impact metrics, shared but privacy-aware datasets, and reproducible analysis pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment and role of research centers and networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous universities and think tanks maintain research centers or interdisciplinary networks dedicated to disinformation research (examples: European Digital Media Observatory, EU DisinfoLab, Shorenstein Center, Stanford Internet Observatory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centers act as hubs for interdisciplinary collaboration, policy engagement, datasets/tools development, and public communication. Evaluating centers includes looking at independence, interdisciplinary composition, and connections to policy actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly publication venues and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists journals that publish credible disinformation research (e.g., Journal of Communication, New Media & Society, Misinformation Review, Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, Social Media + Society, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should aim to publish in established, peer-reviewed outlets; surveys and bibliographic reviews can be used to assess venue relevance. Credibility may be inferred from journal reputation, peer-review standards, and field uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countermeasures and intervention methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Countering disinformation encompasses academic research, critical thinking, digital/media/health/information literacy, fact‑checking, truth‑sandwich approaches, watchdog journalism, science communication, and policy guides (e.g., evidence-based policy recommendations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interventions should be evidence-based and matched to the mechanism (e.g., prebunking for cognitive susceptibility, platform policies for coordinated abuse). Evaluation of interventions requires empirical impact assessment and consideration of free-speech tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of politicisation and funding/policy vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: The field is subject to politicisation and policy controversy (examples include political attacks on researchers, concerns about censorship, and actions such as the NSF withdrawing support for certain disinformation research activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and institutions should consider how political contexts affect funding, perceived legitimacy, and the design/communication of research; transparency, normative grounding, and careful framing can mitigate some politicization risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on evidence-based, bibliographic growth, and historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: The field provides evidence-based research on impacts and counter-strategies; bibliographic analyses show rapid growth since about 2016 with surges around events like COVID-19; disinformation has historical precedents informing modern study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good research situates findings within historical patterns, uses bibliographic and meta-analytic methods to synthesize evidence, and documents growth and shifting emphases across time and topic areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy and cataloguing of mechanisms and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: The field catalogs mechanisms/tactics (psychological, computational, economic, and tactical) such as cognitive bias, echo chambers, bots, astroturfing, deepfakes, clickbait, coordinated inauthentic behavior, ad fraud, and propaganda techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating and using taxonomies helps classify interventions, detection methods, and policy responses. Research should define operational indicators for tactics and link taxonomy items to measurement and mitigation strategies.
